script.opening: "Hi — so I think the HRT’s disagreed with me. I’ve started bleeding again, like having periods back, and it’s been going on over a month now. I assumed a bit of spotting was normal at first but it’s getting heavier. I just want to come off the HRT, to be honest — can you stop it for me? I’d rather put up with the hot flushes than deal with this."

facts.text: If clarified: she started CONTINUOUS combined HRT (intended to be bleed-free) 8 months ago — so unscheduled bleeding persisting beyond the first 6 months (NICE NG23, updated April 2026), and NEW heavier bleeding after settling, needs evaluation rather than simply being accepted as "normal HRT spotting".

Unscheduled bleeding in the first 6 months of systemic HRT (or within 3 months of a dose or preparation change) is common and often settles (NICE NG23, updated April 2026). But this is at 8 months, persisting 5 weeks and INCREASING — that pattern (new bleeding after the settling window, or persistent/heavy) is the one that prompts assessment and possible referral.

HIDDEN AGENDA — she wants to STOP HRT not really because of the bleeding but because a friend was recently diagnosed with breast cancer and she’s become frightened the HRT will "give her cancer"; the bleeding is the excuse to quit. She hasn’t voiced the breast-cancer fear. She also genuinely fears the bleeding itself means womb cancer but won’t say so.

If explored: her vasomotor symptoms were severe (drenching night sweats, no sleep, low mood, struggling at work) and HRT transformed her life — so simply stopping it, without addressing both the bleeding safely AND her fears, would return her to misery.

Officially: stop the HRT to end the bleeding. Actually: reassurance about the breast-cancer fear, proper assessment of the bleeding (which she also secretly fears is cancer), and a way to keep symptom control safely.

ice.ideas: The HRT has caused the bleeding and stopping it will fix the problem.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a friend’s recent breast-cancer diagnosis has her frightened HRT causes cancer (the bleeding is her exit excuse); plus an unvoiced fear the bleeding itself is womb cancer.
ice.expectations: For the GP to stop the HRT. What she actually needs: assessment of unscheduled bleeding (not just stopping HRT), honest breast-cancer risk information, and a plan that keeps her symptom control.

cues: "Just stop the HRT for me" — wanting to quit a treatment that transformed her life; an unspoken reason sits behind it.
Bleeding at 8 months on continuous combined HRT, persistent and increasing — beyond the settling window; needs assessment, not dismissal.
Reluctance/vagueness when symptom relief is mentioned — the real driver (breast-cancer fear) waiting to be named.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that unscheduled bleeding on continuous combined HRT that is PERSISTENT beyond the first 6 months (NICE NG23, updated April 2026: or 3 months after a dose or preparation change), or NEW/heavier after initially settling, requires assessment — and does NOT simply stop the HRT and call it solved

Knows which pathway applies: the NICE NG12 endometrial criteria cover postmenopausal bleeding that CANNOT be attributed to HRT, so bleeding on HRT is not a straightforward NG12 referral; it follows the 2024 joint guideline on unscheduled bleeding on HRT (BMS with RCOG, BGCS, BSGE, CoSRH and RCGP), which NG12 and NG23 signpost — prolonged or heavy bleeding → urgent transvaginal ultrasound within 6 weeks; a uniform endometrium of 4 mm or less on continuous combined HRT is low risk; thicker, or one major or three minor risk factors → suspected cancer referral for biopsy or hysteroscopy

Takes a proper bleeding and HRT history: regimen and duration, adherence (missed progesterone → bleeding/endometrial risk), the exact pattern, and arranges/encourages pelvic/speculum examination and cervical screening status check

Surfaces and addresses the BREAST-CANCER fear (the real driver): gives honest, proportionate information — combined HRT is associated with a small increased breast-cancer risk that depends on type/duration and must be weighed against her severe symptoms — without dismissing or overstating

Avoids the trap of simply stopping effective HRT: explains that quitting would return her to severe symptoms and would NOT remove the need to investigate the bleeding; offers to optimise the regimen safely while the bleeding is assessed
Hears that "stop the HRT" carries an unspoken fear and gently explores it, rather than just actioning the request; validates the breast-cancer worry prompted by her friend
Holds a shared-decision stance: respects her autonomy to stop if she chooses, while ensuring she decides with accurate information and that the bleeding is assessed regardless

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges examination/endometrial assessment/referral as indicated, advises on heavier bleeding/pain, addresses smoking, and books follow-up to review both the bleeding result and her symptom control — a complete plan, not a prescription stop

worked.txt: "I can absolutely stop the HRT if that’s what you decide — but before we do, two things matter. First, the HRT gave you your sleep and your life back, so I don’t want to send you back to those drenching nights without thinking it through. And second, stopping it wouldn’t actually answer the question your bleeding is asking. Let’s do this properly."

"Some unscheduled bleeding in the first few months of this kind of HRT is normal and settles. But yours is at eight months, it’s gone on five weeks, and it’s getting heavier — that pattern I don’t just accept. It needs checking: an examination, and a scan of the womb lining within the next few weeks. The NICE menopause guideline (NG23) and the specialist societies’ 2024 guidance on bleeding on HRT both cover this, and it’s about making sure nothing’s being missed, not about scaring you."

"Can I gently ask what’s really behind wanting to stop? … Your friend’s breast cancer. I’m so sorry — that’s frightening, and it makes complete sense it’s changed how you feel about the HRT. I’m really glad you’ve told me, because now we can talk about the actual numbers rather than the fear."

"Here’s the honest picture: this type of HRT does carry a small increase in breast-cancer risk, it rises the longer you take it, and some of the extra risk lasts for years after stopping. Patches lower the risk of clots compared with tablets, but they don’t change the breast risk. But ‘small’ genuinely means small, and it sits against symptoms that were wrecking your sleep, mood and work. It’s your choice — my job is to make sure you’re choosing with the real figures, not the worst-case in your head. We can also look at lower-risk options."

"So let’s separate them. The bleeding gets assessed whatever you decide about the HRT — that’s non-negotiable for your safety. The HRT decision we make calmly, with the real risk in front of us, and there may be a tweak that suits you better. You don’t have to trade your sleep for your peace of mind."

"I’ll arrange the examination and the womb-lining scan, and refer on if needed. If the bleeding gets much heavier or you get pain, contact us sooner. Cutting down the cigarettes helps your overall risk too, and I can support that. Let’s talk again once we have the scan — we’ll decide the HRT together then. Does that feel okay?"

f.learning: Unscheduled bleeding on HRT is not automatically "just the HRT". Bleeding in the first 6 months of continuous combined HRT (or within 3 months of a dose or preparation change) is common and usually settles (NICE NG23, updated April 2026); but bleeding that PERSISTS beyond that window, or is NEW/heavier after settling, requires assessment — examination, endometrial assessment (TVUSS), and referral per the 2024 joint guideline on unscheduled bleeding on HRT (the NICE NG12 endometrial criteria cover postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT, so NG12 is not the route for bleeding on HRT; the joint guideline decides who needs a suspected cancer referral). The classic error is simply stopping the HRT and considering the problem solved — which both abandons the investigation the bleeding demands and returns the patient to severe symptoms. The examinable hidden agenda is that "stop the HRT" is driven by a friend’s breast-cancer diagnosis and an unspoken fear that HRT (and the bleeding) means cancer. Surface it, give honest proportionate breast-cancer risk information weighed against her severe symptoms, separate the two problems (the bleeding is assessed regardless; the HRT decision is made calmly with real numbers), and keep her symptom control safe.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG23 (updated April 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BMS/RCOG/BGCS/BSGE/CoSRH/RCGP joint guideline on unscheduled bleeding on HRT (2024) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (August 2019) · NICE NG209
knowledge.summary: Bleeding on continuous combined HRT beyond the first 6 months, or new, prolonged or heavier bleeding, needs assessment. Stopping the HRT does not replace that assessment.

points.t: NICE NG23: bleeding is a common side effect in the first 6 months of systemic HRT, or within 3 months of changing dose or preparation; people should seek help promptly for unscheduled bleeding beyond these windows. She is at 8 months with 5 weeks of increasing bleeding.

NICE NG12 endometrial criteria cover postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT. Bleeding on HRT follows the joint BMS-led guideline (2024), which NICE NG12 signposts. She is 54 and on HRT, so assess via that route rather than labelling it a straightforward NICE NG12 referral.

Prolonged or heavy bleeding (or 2 minor risk factors) → urgent transvaginal ultrasound within 6 weeks. A uniform endometrium of 4 mm or less on continuous combined HRT is low risk; above that, refer on the suspected cancer pathway for biopsy or hysteroscopy. One major or three minor risk factors (e.g. BMI 30–39, diabetes) → suspected cancer referral whatever the timing. Her BMI of 29 and smoking are not listed risk factors.
Adherence (missed progesterone increases endometrial risk), patch use, drug interactions, the exact bleeding pattern, speculum examination and cervical screening status.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (August 2019): combined HRT increases breast cancer risk, the increase rises with duration of use and some excess risk persists for years after stopping. NICE NG23 (2024 evidence review) found insufficient evidence that micronised progesterone changes this risk. Present it as small in absolute terms and weigh it against her symptoms, using the NG23 decision aid.
NICE NG209: give very brief advice and offer referral to stop-smoking support with behavioural support and pharmacotherapy.

dg.d: Open question; acknowledged the request to stop without actioning it immediately.
Impact of vasomotor symptoms on sleep, mood and work; her friend’s diagnosis; smoking.
Speculum examination; cervical screening status; urgent TVUS within 6 weeks per BMS 2024.
Endometrial hyperplasia or cancer vs benign HRT-related bleeding, polyp, adherence problem.
Adherence, pattern, pain, post-coital bleeding, discharge; recognised bleeding beyond the NG23 window.
Unscheduled bleeding on continuous combined HRT needing endometrial assessment.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Investigation regardless of the HRT decision; honest breast risk with the NG23 decision aid; her choice to continue.
Smoking cessation offered (NICE NG209); knew thickened endometrium → suspected cancer pathway.
Heavy bleeding, pain or faintness → same day; review with scan result to decide HRT.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “just stop it” despite HRT transforming her life, and explored the reason.
Idea that HRT caused the bleeding; hidden fears of breast and womb cancer; expected HRT to be stopped.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a friend’s recent breast-cancer diagnosis has her frightened HRT causes cancer (the bleeding is her exit excuse); plus an unvoiced fear the bleeding itself is womb cancer — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Wu, it’s Dr Lee returning your call. Can I just confirm your date of birth? Thanks. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Telephone identity check, then open question

model.text: The HRT’s disagreed with me. I’ve been bleeding again for over a month, and it’s getting heavier. I just want to come off it. Can you stop it for me?

I can hear you’ve had enough of it. I’ll make sure we talk about stopping — that’s your choice. First I’d like to understand the bleeding, because that matters whatever we decide about the HRT. Is that okay?
model.why: Respects autonomy while separating the bleeding from the HRT decision

model.text: Fine.
Which HRT are you on, how long, and how do you take it?
A patch, and progesterone capsules every day. Eight months now.
Have there been any days you’ve missed the capsules, or times the patch came off?
model.why: Adherence — missed progestogen raises endometrial risk

model.text: No, I’m good with them. Never missed.
Tell me about the bleeding itself — when it started, how heavy, and any pain, bleeding after sex, or unusual discharge?
Five weeks ago. Spotting at first, now like a light period most days. No pain, nothing after sex, no discharge.
Before the HRT, how bad were the hot flushes and sweats?
model.why: Establishes the symptom cost of stopping

model.text: Awful. Drenched every night, no sleep, crying at work. The HRT gave me my life back, honestly.
It sounds like it’s really helped. So I’m curious — is it only the bleeding that makes you want to stop, or is something else on your mind?
model.why: Explores the unspoken reason behind the request

model.text: (Pause.) My friend’s just been diagnosed with breast cancer. She was on HRT. I keep thinking I’m giving myself cancer.
I’m so sorry about your friend. That’s frightening, and it makes sense it has changed how you feel. Can I ask — has the bleeding made you worry about anything else?
model.why: Validates the breast-cancer fear and gently checks for a second fear

model.text: Womb cancer. I didn’t want to say it.

Thank you for telling me both. On the bleeding: some bleeding in the first six months of this HRT is common. Yours is at eight months and getting heavier, so national guidance says we check it properly rather than assume. That means an examination and an internal scan of the womb lining, which should happen within six weeks.
model.why: Applies the NG23 window and the BMS 2024 urgent TVUS route

model.text: So it might be cancer?

The chance is low, and the scan is how we find out. If the lining is thin, that’s reassuring. If it’s thicker, you’d be seen urgently by the gynaecology team for a closer look. Stopping the HRT wouldn’t answer that question, so the scan happens either way.
model.why: Honest about risk; explains why stopping HRT is not a substitute

model.text: And the breast cancer?

Honestly: combined HRT does slightly increase breast cancer risk, more the longer you take it. In absolute terms the increase is small. I can go through the actual figures with you using the national decision aid, and weigh them against what the hot flushes were doing to your life. Your friend’s illness is real, but it isn’t your risk.
model.why: Proportionate breast-risk information without dismissing or overstating

model.text: I didn’t know it was small. I thought it was a big risk.

So, two separate things. The bleeding gets checked whatever you decide. The HRT decision is yours, made with the real numbers. You could carry on while we wait for the scan, or stop now if you’d rather — what feels right?
model.why: Shared decision with the investigation kept non-negotiable

model.text: I think I’ll carry on until the scan. I can’t face the sweats again.

That sounds reasonable. I’ll book you in for an examination this week and request the scan. One more thing that genuinely lowers your risks: the cigarettes. Would you like help to stop? The stop-smoking service gives you support and medicines, which works much better than willpower alone.
model.why: Examination and TVUS arranged; very brief advice on smoking (NICE NG209)

model.text: Maybe. Send me the details.

If the bleeding becomes very heavy — soaking through pads hourly — or you get pain or feel faint, contact us the same day. Once we have the scan result, let’s speak again and decide the HRT together. What will you take away from today?
The bleeding gets checked anyway. The breast risk is small and I can see the figures. I don’t have to decide today.
Exactly right. Anything else before we finish?
No. I feel much calmer. Thank you.

social.t: Before HRT, symptoms affected sleep, mood and work. Stopping has real costs that she should weigh.
A close friend’s cancer is a common trigger for stopping HRT. Name it, and separate her risk from her friend’s.

legal.t: She may stop HRT at any time. Make sure she decides with accurate risk information and document the discussion (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Endometrial assessment is a safety step; the HRT decision is shared. Keep the two apart explicitly.
Make sure the scan happens within the 6-week window and the result is acted on.

community.t: NICE NG23 patient decision aid on HRT risks and benefits; Women’s Health Concern (the BMS patient arm); local stop-smoking service.

redFlags: Unscheduled bleeding beyond 6 months of HRT, or within 3 months of a change, persisting (NICE NG23, updated April 2026)
Prolonged or heavy bleeding → urgent TVUS within 6 weeks; endometrium above 4 mm on ccHRT → suspected cancer pathway (BMS 2024)
Missed progestogen, post-coital bleeding, discharge, pelvic pain
psychosocial: Severe vasomotor symptoms before HRT: sleep, mood, work
ice: Idea: HRT caused the bleeding; stopping will fix it
Concern: HRT causing breast cancer; the bleeding meaning womb cancer
Expectation: for the GP to stop the HRT

playbook.diagnosis: “This is unscheduled bleeding on HRT. At eight months and getting heavier, it needs an examination and a scan of the womb lining. Most of the time the result is reassuring.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the scan as measuring the thickness of a carpet. If it’s thin, that’s reassuring. If it’s thicker, a specialist takes a closer look.”

management.reflectIce: “Your friend’s illness has understandably made you frightened of the HRT. Let’s look at your real risk, not the worst case.”
management.psychosocial: Weigh her severe pre-HRT symptoms against a small absolute breast risk; she decides.
sharedPlan: Speculum examination and cervical screening check this week
Urgent TVUS within 6 weeks; suspected cancer pathway if endometrium above 4 mm (BMS 2024)
HRT decision shared, using the NICE NG23 decision aid; smoking cessation offered (NICE NG209)
safetyNet: Very heavy bleeding, pain or faintness → same-day contact
Review after the scan to decide on HRT together

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by doing what the patient asks. Stopping HRT feels patient-centred but leaves the bleeding uninvestigated and the real fear untouched.

items.fail: Stopping the HRT and arranging no assessment.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Bleeding beyond the NG23 window needs examination and endometrial assessment.
items.fix: “The scan happens whatever you decide about the HRT.”

items.fail: Calling it “normal breakthrough bleeding” at 8 months.
items.why: The expected window is the first 6 months, or 3 months after a change (NICE NG23, updated April 2026).
items.fix: Name the window and explain why hers is outside it.

items.fail: Labelling it a NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral without thinking about the HRT, or not knowing the thickness threshold.
items.why: NICE NG12 endometrial criteria cover bleeding not attributable to HRT; bleeding on HRT follows the BMS 2024 route.
items.fix: Urgent TVUS within 6 weeks; above 4 mm on ccHRT → suspected cancer pathway.

items.fail: Never asking why she really wants to stop.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s health beliefs.” The friend’s breast cancer is the driver.
items.fix: “Is it only the bleeding, or is something else on your mind?”

items.fail: Dismissing or overstating the breast-cancer risk.
items.fix: Small absolute increase, rising with duration; offer the NG23 decision aid.

items.fail: No follow-up plan linking the scan result to the HRT decision.
items.why: An incomplete plan is a common failing feedback statement.
items.fix: “Once we have the scan, we’ll speak again and decide together.”

Regimen, duration, adherence, pattern, pain, post-coital bleeding, discharge, symptom burden before HRT.

wordPics.fail: Stops the HRT as requested and considers the bleeding solved; or calls it normal HRT spotting; never learns about the friend; no examination or scan; no safety-net.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: separates the mandatory investigation from the shared HRT decision; checks adherence; explains the thin-lining threshold and what happens if thicker; offers the NG23 decision aid; addresses smoking; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “No problem, stop the HRT and the bleeding should settle.”
avoid.instead: “Stopping won’t answer the question the bleeding is asking. The scan happens either way.”
avoid.why: Stopping HRT is not an investigation and returns her to severe symptoms.

avoid.instead: “In the first six months it’s common. At eight months and getting heavier, we check it.”
avoid.why: NICE NG23 sets the 6-month window; beyond it, bleeding needs assessment.

avoid.dont: “The breast cancer risk is tiny, don’t worry about it.”
avoid.instead: “It does rise slightly, more the longer you take it. Let me show you the real figures.”
avoid.why: Dismissing the risk undermines informed choice; overstating it takes away effective treatment.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Bleeding on continuous combined HRT beyond the first 6 months, or new, prolonged or heavier bleeding, needs assessment. Stopping the HRT does not replace that assessment.

points.t: NICE NG23: bleeding is a common side effect in the first 6 months of systemic HRT, or within 3 months of changing dose or preparation; people should seek help promptly for unscheduled bleeding beyond these windows. She is at 8 months with 5 weeks of increasing bleeding.

NICE NG12 endometrial criteria cover postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT. Bleeding on HRT follows the joint BMS-led guideline (2024), which NICE NG12 signposts. She is 54 and on HRT, so assess via that route rather than labelling it a straightforward NICE NG12 referral.

Prolonged or heavy bleeding (or 2 minor risk factors) → urgent transvaginal ultrasound within 6 weeks. A uniform endometrium of 4 mm or less on continuous combined HRT is low risk; above that, refer on the suspected cancer pathway for biopsy or hysteroscopy. One major or three minor risk factors (e.g. BMI 30–39, diabetes) → suspected cancer referral whatever the timing. Her BMI of 29 and smoking are not listed risk factors.
Adherence (missed progesterone increases endometrial risk), patch use, drug interactions, the exact bleeding pattern, speculum examination and cervical screening status.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (August 2019): combined HRT increases breast cancer risk, the increase rises with duration of use and some excess risk persists for years after stopping. NICE NG23 (2024 evidence review) found insufficient evidence that micronised progesterone changes this risk. Present it as small in absolute terms and weigh it against her symptoms, using the NG23 decision aid.
NICE NG209: give very brief advice and offer referral to stop-smoking support with behavioural support and pharmacotherapy.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the request to stop without actioning it immediately.
Impact of vasomotor symptoms on sleep, mood and work; her friend’s diagnosis; smoking.
Picked up “just stop it” despite HRT transforming her life, and explored the reason.
Idea that HRT caused the bleeding; hidden fears of breast and womb cancer; expected HRT to be stopped.
Speculum examination; cervical screening status; urgent TVUS within 6 weeks per BMS 2024.
Endometrial hyperplasia or cancer vs benign HRT-related bleeding, polyp, adherence problem.
Adherence, pattern, pain, post-coital bleeding, discharge; recognised bleeding beyond the NG23 window.
Unscheduled bleeding on continuous combined HRT needing endometrial assessment.
Investigation regardless of the HRT decision; honest breast risk with the NG23 decision aid; her choice to continue.
Smoking cessation offered (NICE NG209); knew thickened endometrium → suspected cancer pathway.
Heavy bleeding, pain or faintness → same day; review with scan result to decide HRT.

social.t: Before HRT, symptoms affected sleep, mood and work. Stopping has real costs that she should weigh.
A close friend’s cancer is a common trigger for stopping HRT. Name it, and separate her risk from her friend’s.

legal.t: She may stop HRT at any time. Make sure she decides with accurate risk information and document the discussion (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Endometrial assessment is a safety step; the HRT decision is shared. Keep the two apart explicitly.
Make sure the scan happens within the 6-week window and the result is acted on.

community.t: NICE NG23 patient decision aid on HRT risks and benefits; Women’s Health Concern (the BMS patient arm); local stop-smoking service.

redFlags: Unscheduled bleeding beyond 6 months of HRT, or within 3 months of a change, persisting (NICE NG23, updated April 2026)
Prolonged or heavy bleeding → urgent TVUS within 6 weeks; endometrium above 4 mm on ccHRT → suspected cancer pathway (BMS 2024)
Missed progestogen, post-coital bleeding, discharge, pelvic pain
psychosocial: Severe vasomotor symptoms before HRT: sleep, mood, work
ice: Idea: HRT caused the bleeding; stopping will fix it
Concern: HRT causing breast cancer; the bleeding meaning womb cancer
Expectation: for the GP to stop the HRT

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is unscheduled bleeding on HRT. At eight months and getting heavier, it needs an examination and a scan of the womb lining. Most of the time the result is reassuring.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the scan as measuring the thickness of a carpet. If it’s thin, that’s reassuring. If it’s thicker, a specialist takes a closer look.”

management.reflectIce: “Your friend’s illness has understandably made you frightened of the HRT. Let’s look at your real risk, not the worst case.”
management.psychosocial: Weigh her severe pre-HRT symptoms against a small absolute breast risk; she decides.
sharedPlan: Speculum examination and cervical screening check this week
Urgent TVUS within 6 weeks; suspected cancer pathway if endometrium above 4 mm (BMS 2024)
HRT decision shared, using the NICE NG23 decision aid; smoking cessation offered (NICE NG209)
safetyNet: Very heavy bleeding, pain or faintness → same-day contact
Review after the scan to decide on HRT together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by doing what the patient asks. Stopping HRT feels patient-centred but leaves the bleeding uninvestigated and the real fear untouched.

items.fail: Stopping the HRT and arranging no assessment.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Bleeding beyond the NG23 window needs examination and endometrial assessment.
items.fix: “The scan happens whatever you decide about the HRT.”

items.fail: Calling it “normal breakthrough bleeding” at 8 months.
items.why: The expected window is the first 6 months, or 3 months after a change (NICE NG23, updated April 2026).
items.fix: Name the window and explain why hers is outside it.

items.fail: Labelling it a NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral without thinking about the HRT, or not knowing the thickness threshold.
items.why: NICE NG12 endometrial criteria cover bleeding not attributable to HRT; bleeding on HRT follows the BMS 2024 route.
items.fix: Urgent TVUS within 6 weeks; above 4 mm on ccHRT → suspected cancer pathway.

items.fail: Never asking why she really wants to stop.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s health beliefs.” The friend’s breast cancer is the driver.
items.fix: “Is it only the bleeding, or is something else on your mind?”

items.fail: Dismissing or overstating the breast-cancer risk.
items.fix: Small absolute increase, rising with duration; offer the NG23 decision aid.

items.fail: No follow-up plan linking the scan result to the HRT decision.
items.why: An incomplete plan is a common failing feedback statement.
items.fix: “Once we have the scan, we’ll speak again and decide together.”
